client: Hey Luna, I've been really down lately. Last week, I got a rejection letter from my dream university, and I can't shake off this feeling of inadequacy. I know I should be focusing on other options, but it's hard not to feel like I'm just not good enough. I'm not sure if talking about it will really help, but I'm trying to be open to it.
therapist: Hey there, I'm really glad you reached out. It sounds like you're going through a tough time, and it's completely understandable to feel down after such a significant setback. Rejection can really shake our confidence, but it doesn't define your worth or your potential. How have you been coping with these feelings so far?

client: Thanks for listening, Luna. I've mostly been trying to distract myself with other activities, like spending time with friends and family, but it feels like a temporary fix. I keep thinking about what I could have done differently or if I'm just not good enough. It's hard to shake those thoughts.
therapist: I can see that you're putting a lot of effort into coping, and it's great that you're spending time with loved ones. It's natural to have those self-doubts creeping in, especially after a significant disappointment. Have you tried exploring some of the evidence that supports your abilities and strengths? What are some things you're proud of, or that others have recognized in you?

client: I appreciate the suggestion, but it's hard to focus on my strengths right now. I feel like every time I think about my achievements, they seem small and insignificant compared to this rejection. Plus, it feels like I'm just trying to convince myself, and it doesn't really stick. I know I should be more positive, but it's tough.
therapist: I understand that it's really challenging to see your strengths right now, especially when this rejection feels so significant. It's okay to acknowledge that your achievements might seem smaller in comparison, but it doesn't mean they're insignificant. Sometimes, it helps to look at the bigger picture and remember that one setback doesn't erase all your hard work and accomplishments. What are some small steps you think might help you start to rebuild your confidence?

client: I know you're right, but it's hard to see that right now. I guess one small step could be to write down some of my past successes and the positive feedback I've received. But it feels so forced, and I'm not sure if it will make a difference. It's just hard to believe in myself when I feel like I've failed.
therapist: I hear you, and it's completely valid to feel that way. Taking small steps, like writing down your successes and positive feedback, can feel forced at first, but it can gradually help shift your perspective. It's okay to start small and be gentle with yourself. What do you think might make this exercise feel a bit more meaningful or less forced? Maybe there's a specific success or piece of feedback that stands out to you?

client: I think what might make it more meaningful is if I focus on the times when I felt genuinely proud of myself, rather than just listing everything. Maybe I can start with the times when I overcame a significant challenge or when someone I respect told me how much they believed in me. It still feels a bit daunting, but it might help me see that I'm not as inadequate as I feel right now.
therapist: That's a great approach, focusing on the times when you felt genuinely proud can be much more impactful and meaningful. It sounds like you're starting to find a way to connect with your strengths and resilience. Taking it one step at a time, and reflecting on those moments when you overcame challenges or received genuine support, can really help build that sense of self-worth. How about setting aside a few minutes each day to reflect on one of these moments? What do you think might be the first memory you'd like to focus on?

client: I like the idea of reflecting on one memory each day. The first one that comes to mind is when I helped organize a charity event last year. It was a lot of work, but seeing the positive impact it had on the community made me feel really proud and capable. I think focusing on that might help me see that I can make a difference, even if things don't always go as planned. It's still a bit hard to believe, but I'm willing to try.
therapist: That's a wonderful memory to start with. Organizing that charity event and seeing the positive impact it had is a powerful reminder of your capabilities and the good you can do. It's completely normal to still have some doubts, but focusing on these moments can help you build a more balanced view of yourself. How do you think you can carry that sense of pride and capability into your current situation?

client: I think I can try to apply the same determination and effort I put into that charity event to my current situation. It might help me see that I can handle challenges and make a difference, even if things don't always go as planned. But it's still hard to shake the feeling of inadequacy, and I worry that I might just be setting myself up for more disappointment.
therapist: It's really admirable that you're willing to apply that same determination and effort to your current situation. Recognizing that you have the capacity to handle challenges and make a difference is a powerful step. It's completely normal to still feel some inadequacy and worry about future disappointment. These feelings are part of the process, and it's okay to acknowledge them. How can you support yourself as you take on this new challenge, and what might help you manage those feelings of inadequacy?

client: Thanks, Luna. I think having a support system in place will be really important. Talking to friends and family who believe in me can help, and maybe setting smaller, achievable goals to build my confidence. But it's still a struggle to not let those feelings of inadequacy take over. I guess I need to be patient with myself and keep reminding myself of the good things I've done.
therapist: You're doing a great job recognizing the importance of a support system and setting smaller goals to build your confidence. It's completely normal for feelings of inadequacy to still be there, and being patient with yourself is key. Celebrating even the small achievements can help shift your focus and build a more positive outlook over time. What are some specific small goals you'd like to set for yourself, and how can you make them feel achievable and rewarding?

client: I think a small goal could be to apply to a few more universities that I'm interested in, but that feel a bit more attainable. I could also start working on my application essays a little each day. It feels manageable, but I'm still worried about the time and effort it will take, and whether it will all be worth it in the end. I guess I just need to take it one step at a time and try to stay positive.
therapist: It sounds like you're taking a thoughtful and practical approach by setting these smaller, manageable goals. Applying to more attainable universities and working on your application essays bit by bit can really help build your confidence and reduce the feeling of being overwhelmed. It's natural to have some worries about the time and effort, but taking it one step at a time is a great way to stay focused and positive. How do you think you can reward yourself for making progress on these goals, even in small ways?

client: I like the idea of rewarding myself for making progress. Maybe I can treat myself to a favorite snack or some downtime after I work on my applications for a while. It feels a bit indulgent, but I think it could help motivate me to keep going, even when it gets tough.
therapist: That's a fantastic idea! Treating yourself to a favorite snack or some downtime can be a great way to stay motivated and make the process feel more manageable. It's not indulgent at all; it's about acknowledging your hard work and taking care of yourself. How do you think you can build these rewards into your routine to keep yourself motivated, especially during the tougher moments?
